question:
A customer reports a defect in the executable we shipped to them two years ago, and to investigate it we need that very same executable back, byte for byte, but the toolchain and third-party libraries on our machines have been upgraded since then. What should the team have been tracking and preserving so that this would be possible?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).

## Guidelines for Preserving What Is Needed to Reproduce a Past Shipped Executable

---

### 1. Place every software configuration item (SCI) under version control — including source code, configuration files, and related artifacts

The first step in being able to reproduce any past build is ensuring that all software items that contribute to the final product are tracked from the very beginning. Version control [SWEBOK excerpt 54c795b57ddb8260db0c]," and "[SWEBOK excerpt 7b5ea5486a11b3f72ba3]."

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt 5e4a6e602c049ac774e7]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Configuration Management and Change Control/Software Configuration Management Tools and Verification Activities.md`)

---

### 2. Place the build tools (compilers, linkers, etc.) and their associated build instructions under SCM control

The toolchain — compilers and all supporting tools — is itself a configuration item that must be version-controlled. The SWEBOK explicitly states: "[SWEBOK excerpt e082f1c815b2042b56a6]."

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt e082f1c815b2042b56a6]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Software Build Tools and Version Control Management.md`)

---

### 3. Manage purchased/third-party software products (libraries, compilers) under configuration control as part of SCM planning

Third-party libraries and tools are not exempt from configuration management. SCM planning must explicitly consider "[SWEBOK excerpt e65119b1f59c88c327c0]." If those libraries upgrade silently, you lose the ability to reproduce the original build.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt c963e608b16aa4174e20]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Interface Control/SCM Workbenches and Vendor Control Planning.md`)

---

### 4. Establish and maintain a formally identified product baseline at the time of each release

A baseline is the stable, controlled reference point that marks the exact state of all configuration items at a given moment — the product as shipped. The SWEBOK notes that "baselines are identified where stability is intended," and that successful configuration [SWEBOK excerpt 884d3b2a83ee216846ae]." Without a formally established baseline, there is no authoritative record of what was actually shipped.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt 02abc792344d2a2bf644]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Configuration Management and Change Control/Baselines and Change Management in Configuration Control.md`)

---

### 5. Preserve build outputs (binaries/executables) in a controlled binary repository

Beyond preserving what is needed to *re-build*, the team should also store the actual build artifacts themselves. The CMS includes "a repository [that] [SWEBOK excerpt 9f109b518ac9ba33baaa]." Storing the executable directly means it can be retrieved byte-for-byte without any need to re-build at all.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt 93cb0cdc79d239bdea25]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Configuration Management System Tools and Components.md`)

---

### 6. Produce and retain a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and build outputs as formal CM records

The SWEBOK identifies the SBOM as "an important CM output" that lists the artifacts included in a build. Retaining this record for each release documents exactly what components were part of the executable, enabling traceability back to that specific build. Moreover, "[SWEBOK excerpt 626e98b737e85a1b3bcb]" and "[SWEBOK excerpt a4ef685722d26ada8f79]."

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt 450578f233490c4cd9fa]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Build Quality Assurance and Configuration Management/Software Build Artifacts and Continuous Integration Processes.md`; and *"[SWEBOK excerpt a35fff3110753b6e55b1]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Build Quality Assurance and Configuration Management/Build Process Quality Verification and Documentation.md`)

---

### 7. Conduct a Physical Configuration Audit (PCA) before shipping to ensure the as-built product matches its documentation

A [SWEBOK excerpt 0f3e2954a6ce66de5a11]." Performing this audit at release time creates a verified, auditable record that the shipped executable corresponds to the controlled baseline — giving investigators a trustworthy anchor when a defect surfaces later.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt 7c05dcb6f5d4ac05c82b]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Software Configuration Auditing and Verification/Software Configuration Audits for Quality Assurance.md`)

---

### 8. Document and preserve the Version Description Document (VDD) for every release

The VDD is the formal record of exactly what was packaged and delivered. The SWEBOK states: "[SWEBOK excerpt 7ea550447dc0afcc450c])." Combined with release notes that describe "[SWEBOK excerpt 4de3a61399f81219b406] VDD gives investigators a complete picture of what was in the release and what environment it was intended for.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt 1bc7457ba6b688fca089])."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Software Release Management and Deployment Processes.md`; and *"[SWEBOK excerpt 85b9d768031986a6736e]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/Release Management Tools and Documentation Requirements.md`)

---

### 9. Maintain Configuration Status Accounting (SCSA) records that track the history of baselines, change requests, and their disposition

SCSA "records and reports [SWEBOK excerpt 3980cfd77cf16eba8e23]." Its records include "[SWEBOK excerpt 6de1b499ea67b4827b26]," and "impacted CIs and related systems." These records let the team trace exactly which change requests (SCRs) were incorporated into the released baseline, connecting the customer's defect report to the precise code that was shipped.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt e41db48f02d215e51652]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Configuration Status Accounting and Reporting/Configuration Status Accounting and Management Reporting/Deviations, Waivers, and Configuration Status Accounting.md`)

---

### 10. Explicitly plan to retain the ability to reproduce previous releases as a named SCM requirement

Reproducing old releases must be a deliberate, planned objective — not an afterthought. The SWEBOK is unambiguous: "[SWEBOK excerpt 2fd1831ea30e710b92d8]." This expectation should be written into the SCM Plan (SCMP) and honoured throughout the product's lifecycle.

(source: *"[SWEBOK excerpt ed245abb0f39c360af98]."* — `/workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Configuration Management Planning and Implementation/Software Configuration Management Tools and Processes/In-Process Audits and Software Release Management.md`)

---

**Summary.** The SWEBOK's Software Configuration Management knowledge area makes clear that reproducing a past executable requires a layered strategy: version-controlling all source and configuration items, putting the entire toolchain (compilers, build tools, third-party libraries) under the same CM discipline, formally baselining and auditing the release, storing the binary artifacts directly, capturing the VDD/SBOM as release records, and maintaining status accounting history — all underpinned by an explicit SCM plan that names release reproducibility as a standing requirement.
